subtopic_detail: Bruising over the cheek with a torn upper lip frenulum in a four month old who cannot yet roll
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar asked by the emergency department to review a four month old boy brought in by both parents because of a bruise on his face. They say he rolled off the change table onto carpet yesterday afternoon while his father turned to get a nappy.

He has not yet rolled at home according to the parent held record and his development is otherwise age appropriate. He is feeding well, is up to date with immunisations and has never been seen here before. His mother mentions that he has been fussy with feeds for two days and that a little blood appeared on the teat of the bottle this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: A 2 cm purple bruise over the left cheek and a second smaller bruise over the left ear helix, a torn upper lip frenulum with fresh clot, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no hepatosplenomegaly, no other marks on full skin inspection, tone and moro reflex normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (100-140), platelets 342 x10^9/L (150-450), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.9-1.3), activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds (25-38)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit him for a skeletal survey and neuroimaging with ophthalmology review, and notify statutory child protection services before any discharge
options.rationale: Bruising in an infant who is not independently mobile, bruising of the ear and a torn frenulum are each high specificity markers of inflicted injury, and together they mandate admission for occult injury screening and a statutory report. Admission also provides a place of safety while the assessment proceeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey for later in the week and discharge him home with his parents once the bruising has been documented
options.rationale: Deferring the survey sends the child back to the environment in which the injury occurred and loses the paired imaging and clinical assessment that occult fracture detection depends on. Timing of the statutory report cannot wait on imaging logistics. (Source: Queensland Health: Child protection guideline)

options.text: Order a skeletal survey and a clotting profile now, and if both are normal reassure the parents and arrange general practitioner follow up
options.rationale: Normal investigations do not exclude inflicted injury, because most abusive head trauma and many soft tissue injuries leave no radiological trace. Making the report conditional on abnormal imaging inverts the threshold, which is reasonable suspicion rather than proof. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Photograph the bruises, repeat the coagulation screen in one week and review him in the paediatric outpatient clinic
options.rationale: A normal coagulation screen has already been obtained and repeating it a week later neither explains the frenulum tear nor protects the child in the interval. Bleeding disorders cause bruising in unusual sites but do not tear a frenulum in a baby who cannot bring objects forcefully to his mouth. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Accept the history of a fall, give written head injury advice and ask the child health nurse to visit the family at home this week
options.rationale: The history is not consistent with the injuries, since a baby who has never rolled cannot generate the mechanism described and carpet does not tear a frenulum. Accepting an implausible history is the commonest single failure in these presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in an infant who is not yet independently mobile is the single most useful red flag in child protection paediatrics, because babies who cannot roll, crawl or cruise do not sustain accidental bruises. The sites here compound that concern, since the ear and the cheek are protected areas rarely struck in falls, and a torn upper lip frenulum in a pre mobile baby is strongly associated with forced feeding or a direct blow. The history is discrepant in two ways, describing a developmental milestone the child has not reached and a mechanism that cannot produce an intraoral injury. Management is admission for a skeletal survey, neuroimaging and dilated fundoscopy to find occult fractures and intracranial or retinal haemorrhage, together with a statutory notification made on suspicion rather than on proof. A normal coagulation screen makes an inherited bleeding disorder unlikely but never substitutes for the protection assessment.
key_points: Any bruise in an infant who cannot independently move demands explanation and usually investigation.
Ear, neck, torso and intraoral injuries are high specificity sites for inflicted trauma.
A history describing a milestone the child has not reached is a discrepant history.
Occult injury screening in an infant includes skeletal survey, neuroimaging and fundoscopy.
Statutory notification is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not by confirmed investigation results.
explanation.pearls: A skeletal survey in a child under two is repeated at eleven to fourteen days, because healing periosteal reaction makes rib and metaphyseal fractures visible that were invisible on the first films, and omitting the repeat films is a recognised source of missed diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase of 12400 in a four year old boy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a four year old boy whose parents are worried that he walks on his toes and cannot keep up with his older cousins. He falls more than other children at kindergarten and his teacher has noticed he pushes on his thighs to get up from sitting on the floor.

He walked at eighteen months and says short sentences that his family understand. His calves look bulky compared with his thighs. You arranged blood tests at the last visit and the results are now available.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait with toe walking, bulky firm calves, proximal weakness with a positive Gowers manoeuvre, reflexes present at the knees and reduced at the ankles, no fasciculation and no sensory deficit
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 12400 units per litre (60-305), alanine aminotransferase 180 units per litre (10-40), aspartate aminotransferase 210 units per litre (10-45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an orthopaedic surgeon for serial casting of the ankles to correct the toe walking and to improve his gait pattern
options.rationale: Casting treats idiopathic toe walking, in which strength and creatine kinase are normal, and here it would immobilise a boy whose weakness is progressive. Periods of immobilisation accelerate loss of ambulation in dystrophinopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer him for an open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps for dystrophin immunostaining before any other investigation is undertaken
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for the minority whose genetic testing is uninformative, since it needs a general anaesthetic and adds little when a deletion is found. Ordering it first exposes the child to an avoidable procedure. (Source: Muscular Dystrophy Australia: Diagnosis pathway)

options.text: Repeat the liver enzymes and arrange a liver ultrasound, since the raised transaminases suggest an underlying hepatic disorder in this child
options.rationale: Transaminases are released from damaged skeletal muscle as well as from liver, and chasing them here is the classic diversion that delays neuromuscular diagnosis by months. A gamma glutamyl transferase would be normal and would settle the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant of gait in preschool children and repeat the creatine kinase measurement in six months
options.rationale: Toe walking with proximal weakness and a creatine kinase in the thousands is never a normal variant, and delay costs the window in which corticosteroids best preserve ambulation. Idiopathic toe walkers have normal strength and can stand from the floor without their hands. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric neurology service for genetic testing of the dystrophin gene with genetic counselling for the family
options.rationale: Genetic analysis for deletions, duplications and then sequence variants confirms the diagnosis non invasively in the great majority of boys and is the entry point to corticosteroid therapy, cardiac and respiratory surveillance and variant specific treatments. It also allows carrier testing of female relatives. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy presents in boys between two and five years with delayed motor milestones, toe walking, a waddling gait and difficulty rising from the floor, and calf pseudohypertrophy reflects replacement of muscle by fat and connective tissue. A creatine kinase in the thousands to tens of thousands is the screening test, and transaminases are commonly raised from muscle rather than liver, a finding that regularly sends children down a hepatology pathway first. Confirmation is genetic, using multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification for deletions and duplications followed by sequencing, with muscle biopsy reserved for genetically uninformative cases. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong ambulation, and cardiac and respiratory surveillance begins well before symptoms. A positive Gowers manoeuvre in a preschool boy should prompt a creatine kinase on the same day.
key_points: Calf pseudohypertrophy with proximal weakness in a boy suggests a dystrophinopathy.
Creatine kinase is the screening test and is typically above ten thousand units per litre.
Raised transaminases in this setting usually come from muscle, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms it.
Genetic testing has replaced biopsy as the first confirmatory test.
Corticosteroids and cardiorespiratory surveillance begin early, so delay has a real cost.
explanation.pearls: Girls are not exempt: manifesting carriers can present with calf hypertrophy, cramps and a creatine kinase of several thousand, and every female relative identified through cascade testing needs cardiac surveillance because cardiomyopathy can occur without any skeletal muscle weakness.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and poor weight gain at five weeks with sodium 122 and potassium 7.1
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a five week old boy brought in with four days of vomiting after feeds. His mother describes the vomit as milky and forceful and says he seems hungry again straight afterwards.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and was discharged on day two. He now weighs 3.4 kg, having been 3.6 kg at birth. He is drowsy but rousable, with a dry mouth and reduced skin turgor. The surgical registrar has been asked to see him for a suspected pyloric problem and the blood results have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle with delayed capillary refill, deeply pigmented scrotum and areolae, testes descended with a normally formed penis, no palpable abdominal mass, abdomen soft with active bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 7.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), chloride 112 mmol/L (98-110), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (18-26), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-6.5), creatinine 58 micromol/L (20-50), glucose 2.4 mmol/L (3.5-6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood for a steroid profile then give intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and dextrose without waiting for the hormone results
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, acidosis and hypoglycaemia in a shocked infant is a salt wasting crisis until proven otherwise, and glucocorticoid replacement with volume and glucose is both diagnostic and lifesaving. The sample taken beforehand preserves the diagnosis for later confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

options.text: Start intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin after blood and urine cultures and give a fluid bolus while awaiting the septic screen results
options.rationale: Sepsis is a reasonable parallel concern in a collapsed infant and cultures with empirical cover are appropriate, but antibiotics alone will not reverse a crisis driven by absent cortisol and aldosterone. The electrolyte triad points away from sepsis as the sole explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give an intravenous fluid bolus and correct the alkalosis with sodium chloride and added potassium before the surgical team proceeds to theatre
options.rationale: The classical metabolic picture of gastric outlet obstruction is a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis, and this child has the mirror image with a low bicarbonate, a high chloride and a high potassium. Adding potassium to a baby with a level above seven would be dangerous. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

options.text: Start an insulin and dextrose infusion with nebulised salbutamol to shift the potassium intracellularly and repeat the electrolytes hourly
options.rationale: Shifting potassium treats a number rather than the disease driving it, and in mineralocorticoid deficiency the potassium climbs straight back once the infusion stops. These measures are adjuncts reserved for arrhythmia or extreme levels while definitive hormone and salt replacement is being given. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Take blood for a steroid profile and start oral fludrocortisone with additional salt supplements once he has tolerated a feed without vomiting
options.rationale: Oral therapy cannot be absorbed reliably by a shocked vomiting infant, and fludrocortisone alone does not provide the glucocorticoid activity needed to support blood pressure and glucose in crisis. It becomes part of long term maintenance once the child is stable. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia presents in the second to fifth week of life, and boys are the ones who present in crisis because they have no ambiguity of the genitalia to prompt earlier diagnosis. The combination of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and hypoglycaemia is close to specific, and hyperpigmentation from high adrenocorticotrophic hormone is a useful bedside clue. The trap in this vignette is the forceful milky vomiting of a five week old boy, which points to gastric outlet obstruction, but that condition produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis, so the biochemistry disconfirms it outright. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone with sodium chloride and dextrose after a sample is taken for seventeen hydroxyprogesterone, renin and cortisol, since delaying steroid for the result risks cardiac arrest. Newborn screening for this condition is not performed in all Australian jurisdictions, so clinical recognition remains essential.
key_points: Low sodium with high potassium, acidosis and hypoglycaemia in an infant means adrenal crisis until excluded.
Gastric outlet obstruction gives the opposite biochemistry, a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis.
Boys with salt wasting disease have normal genitalia and therefore present later and sicker.
Take the diagnostic sample first, then give hydrocortisone without waiting for the result.
Hydrocortisone in stress doses supplies the mineralocorticoid effect needed acutely.
explanation.pearls: Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis resolves with hydrocortisone and saline, so calcium gluconate is reserved for electrocardiographic changes, and the commonest iatrogenic error is adding potassium to maintenance fluids after the initial correction because the number has fallen quickly.

subtopic_detail: Systolic murmur with weak femoral pulses at the six week check in a thriving infant
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing the six week check on a baby girl who is feeding well and has gained 900 g since birth. Her mother has no concerns and the pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated.

On auscultation you hear a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge that radiates to the back. The brachial pulses are easy to feel but you cannot confidently feel either femoral pulse. She is pink in room air, is not tachypnoeic and the liver edge is not enlarged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in the right hand and 96 per cent in the right foot, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge radiating to the interscapular area, brachial pulses normal volume, femoral pulses not palpable, no hepatomegaly, no sweating with feeds, capillary refill under two seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral frusemide for early heart failure and arrange paediatric cardiology review within the following week with weight monitoring
options.rationale: There is no hepatomegaly, tachypnoea or feeding sweat to indicate failure, and diuresis in a baby dependent on preload for systemic perfusion can precipitate collapse. Medication is not a substitute for defining the anatomy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Reassure the mother that this has the features of an innocent murmur and review the baby at the next scheduled immunisation visit
options.rationale: Innocent murmurs are never accompanied by absent femoral pulses, and radiation through to the back is not a feature of a venous hum or a Still murmur. Reassurance here risks presentation in shock when the arterial duct finishes closing. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Arrange assessment by a paediatric service the same day, with four limb blood pressures and echocardiography before she goes home
options.rationale: Absent femoral pulses with a murmur radiating to the back is aortic obstruction until disproved, and the diagnosis must be made before ductal tissue completes its closure and precipitates collapse. Four limb pressures and echocardiography define the lesion and its severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease)

options.text: Order an electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph today and review the baby in the surgery once both results have become available
options.rationale: Both tests can be normal in early coarctation and neither changes the immediate decision, so they add delay without adding safety. Imaging that answers the question is echocardiography performed by a service that can act on it. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease)

options.text: Refer her to the paediatric cardiology clinic as a routine appointment and advise the mother to return sooner if feeding or breathing worsens
options.rationale: A routine wait of weeks straddles exactly the period in which critical obstruction declares itself, and parents cannot reliably detect the transition until the infant is already shocked. Urgency is set by the pulse finding, not by how well the baby currently looks. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

explanation.summary: Coarctation of the aorta is the congenital lesion most often missed at the newborn and six week checks, because a baby with a patent arterial duct can perfuse the lower body normally and look entirely well. As the duct closes over the first weeks the obstruction is unmasked, and the infant who was thriving presents collapsed with acidosis and absent pulses. Palpation of the femoral pulses at every routine check is therefore the single highest yield part of the cardiovascular examination in infancy, and a murmur radiating to the interscapular area strengthens the suspicion. Pre and post ductal saturation difference may be small or absent once the duct has largely closed, so a normal pulse oximetry screen does not exclude the diagnosis. Referral for same day paediatric assessment with four limb blood pressures and echocardiography is the correct pathway, and prostaglandin is given if the infant decompensates.
key_points: Absent or weak femoral pulses in an infant means aortic obstruction until echocardiography says otherwise.
A thriving well baby does not exclude coarctation while the arterial duct remains open.
A murmur radiating to the back is a specific and easily missed clue.
Newborn pulse oximetry screening misses many coarctations.
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph are frequently normal early and should not delay referral.
explanation.pearls: Compare the right arm and either leg blood pressure rather than left arm and leg, because an aberrant or coarcted left subclavian origin can make the left arm pressure falsely low, and a gradient above twenty mmHg between right arm and leg supports the diagnosis.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic episodes triggered by crying with rapid recovery and a normal electrocardiogram at fifteen months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a fifteen month old girl who has had six frightening episodes over three months. Each begins when she is upset, after a fall or when a toy is taken away.

Her mother describes a long silent cry, then the lips turning blue, then a few seconds of limpness before she comes round and wants a cuddle. She is back to normal within a minute and has never been sleepy afterwards. She is fully immunised, her development is normal and an electrocardiogram arranged by the general practitioner was reported as normal with a normal corrected QT interval.

data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, pale conjunctivae, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiac examination with no murmur, normal tone and power with age appropriate gait, developmental milestones appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to look for an epileptiform focus that could explain the recurrent episodes of limpness and colour change
options.rationale: The episodes are consistently provoked by an emotional or painful trigger and recovery is immediate without a postictal phase, which is not the pattern of epilepsy. An electroencephalogram in this setting is more likely to produce an incidental finding than an answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram with video recording and review her in the neurology clinic when the report is available
options.rationale: Adding sleep deprivation and video increases the sensitivity of a test that is not indicated, since the diagnosis here is clinical and the trigger is stereotyped. The delay also leaves a treatable contributor unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram to exclude a structural cardiac cause for the cyanosis and the transient loss of postural tone during the episodes
options.rationale: Structural disease severe enough to cause cyanotic episodes would give an abnormal cardiac examination or persisting symptoms between events rather than colour change confined to crying. The normal examination and electrocardiogram make this a low yield test. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Send a full blood count with ferritin, since correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency of these episodes in a substantial proportion of children
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is common in children with these spells and treating it reduces their frequency, making it the one investigation that changes management. The pale conjunctivae in this child strengthen the case for testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Send a venous blood gas with lactate and an ammonia level during a well period to screen for an underlying metabolic disorder causing the events
options.rationale: Metabolic decompensation presents with intercurrent illness, poor feeding and developmental regression rather than brief episodes tied to frustration. Sampling between episodes in a thriving child with normal development adds nothing. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect around five per cent of children between six months and five years and are diagnosed on the history alone, with a provoking event, a cry, apnoea in expiration, colour change and then brief limpness or stiffening. The cyanotic type follows anger or frustration, while the pallid type follows a minor knock and reflects a vagally mediated asystolic pause. Rapid recovery without a postictal state separates them from seizures, although a brief anoxic convulsion at the end of a long spell does not change the diagnosis. Iron deficiency with or without anaemia is over represented in affected children, and iron supplementation reduces the frequency of spells, which makes a full blood count with ferritin the only routine test worth doing beyond an electrocardiogram. Parents need explicit reassurance that the episodes are involuntary, that the child is not manipulating them and that the condition resolves by school age.
key_points: Diagnosis rests on a stereotyped trigger, a cry, colour change and immediate recovery.
An electrocardiogram excludes long QT syndrome, particularly in pallid episodes.
Full blood count and ferritin are the only other routine tests required.
Iron replacement reduces spell frequency even when haemoglobin is normal.
Absence of a postictal phase distinguishes these events from epileptic seizures.
explanation.pearls: Advise parents to lay the child flat on their side during a spell rather than picking them up or shaking them, because the upright posture prolongs cerebral hypoperfusion and recovery, and warn them that a short stiffening jerk at the end of a spell is anoxic rather than epileptic and needs no anticonvulsant.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks

subtopic_detail: Breech presentation at term as the only risk factor for hip dysplasia in a newborn with a normal examination
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward reviewing a two day old girl before discharge. She was born at thirty nine weeks by caesarean section for a persistent breech presentation and has fed well since birth.

There is no family history of hip problems and the pregnancy was otherwise unremarkable with normal liquor volume. Her mother asks whether anything needs to be arranged for the hips because a friend's baby was put in a harness.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical thigh creases, full and equal abduction of both hips, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing, legs of equal length on Galeazzi testing, spine and feet normal, neurological examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her hips?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic radiograph now to assess the acetabular index and refer to the orthopaedic clinic if the femoral head appears displaced
options.rationale: The femoral head is unossified in the newborn, so radiography cannot assess it and only becomes useful from about four to six months of age. It also delivers gonadal irradiation for no diagnostic return. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Refer her for fitting of a Pavlik harness now on the basis of the breech presentation and review her in the orthopaedic clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: A harness treats dysplasia that has been demonstrated, not a risk factor alone, and unnecessary abduction bracing carries a risk of avascular necrosis. The decision to treat follows the ultrasound. (Source: Healthy Hips Australia: Clinical information)

options.text: Reassure her mother that the normal newborn examination excludes the condition and arrange no imaging beyond the routine child health checks
options.rationale: Clinical examination misses dysplastic hips that are located and stable at birth, which is precisely why risk factor based imaging exists. A normal examination lowers but does not remove the risk conferred by breech presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at around six weeks of age and continue routine clinical examination of the hips at each scheduled review
options.rationale: Breech presentation in the third trimester warrants imaging even when the examination is normal, and ultrasound at six weeks to four months avoids the false positives of scanning newborn physiological laxity. Clinical examination continues because dysplasia can appear later. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward and refer to orthopaedics if any measurement falls outside the normal range
options.rationale: Scanning in the first weeks detects physiological immaturity that resolves spontaneously, generating harnesses and reviews that the child never needed. The window that balances sensitivity against false positives opens at about six weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for clinically at every newborn and infant check, but clinical examination alone misses a substantial proportion of dysplastic hips that are neither dislocated nor dislocatable. Australian practice therefore adds selective ultrasound for defined risk factors, of which breech presentation in the third trimester and a first degree family history are the strongest. Timing matters in both directions, because scanning in the first weeks captures physiological laxity that would have resolved and leads to overtreatment, while a pelvic radiograph is uninterpretable until the femoral head begins to ossify at around four to six months. Ultrasound at six weeks to four months is the compromise that Australian guidelines adopt. Treatment with an abduction harness is reserved for hips shown to be dysplastic or unstable, and late presentation after walking age usually requires operative reduction.
key_points: Breech presentation and a family history are the risk factors that trigger selective imaging.
A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude dysplasia.
Ultrasound is performed at about six weeks, not in the first days of life.
Radiography is uninformative until femoral head ossification at four to six months.
Harness treatment follows demonstrated dysplasia rather than risk factors alone.
explanation.pearls: Limited or asymmetrical hip abduction is the most reliable sign after three months of age, by which time Ortolani and Barlow testing has usually become negative because the soft tissues have tightened around a dislocated hip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
BMJ Best Practice: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: Unimmunised ten month old exposed to measles two days ago in a hospital waiting room
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by the public health unit about a ten month old boy who sat in an emergency department waiting room two days ago at the same time as a person later confirmed to have measles. His parents have declined all immunisations so far but say they are willing to reconsider after this.

He is well today with no fever, rash or coryza. He was born at term, has no medical problems and is not taking any medication. His mother is known to be immune from her own childhood infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, no rash and no conjunctivitis, oral mucosa clear with no Koplik spots, chest clear on auscultation, no lymphadenopathy, growth along the fiftieth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action for this child?

options.text: Give normal human immunoglobulin intramuscularly today and bring forward his first scheduled vaccine appointment to the following week
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is the option when vaccine cannot be used or when more than seventy two hours have elapsed, and it also blunts the response to vaccine given afterwards for several months. Choosing it here forfeits the durable protection available from the vaccine. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: Give the measles mumps and rubella vaccine today, and count this dose as extra to the two doses he still requires from twelve months of age
options.rationale: Vaccine given within seventy two hours of exposure can prevent or attenuate disease and is preferred to immunoglobulin in a healthy infant. A dose before the first birthday does not count towards the schedule because maternal antibody may blunt it. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: Take no specific action now, advise the family about isolation, and review him urgently if fever or rash develops in the next two weeks
options.rationale: Watchful waiting forgoes an intervention that works when given inside the seventy two hour window and leaves a susceptible infant at risk of pneumonia and encephalitis. Isolation advice is necessary but is not sufficient on its own. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG

options.text: Check measles serology today and give the vaccine only if the immunoglobulin G result returns negative for protective antibody levels
options.rationale: Waiting for serology consumes the narrow window in which prophylaxis works, and a positive result in an infant may reflect residual maternal antibody rather than protection. Post exposure decisions are made on exposure history and age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: Defer any vaccine until twelve months of age as scheduled, and give a course of oral vitamin A now to reduce the severity of any illness
options.rationale: Vitamin A reduces mortality in children with established measles rather than preventing infection after exposure, so it does not substitute for prophylaxis. Deferring to the routine schedule ignores the current exposure. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG

explanation.summary: Measles is among the most transmissible infections known, with airborne spread persisting in a room for up to two hours after the case has left, so shared waiting room air counts as a genuine exposure. For a susceptible immunocompetent contact aged six months or older, measles mumps and rubella vaccine given within seventy two hours of first exposure can prevent or modify disease and is preferred to immunoglobulin. Normal human immunoglobulin is used instead when the exposure was more than seventy two hours but within six days, when the contact is under six months, pregnant or significantly immunocompromised, and it delays subsequent vaccination for months. A dose of vaccine given before twelve months of age does not count towards the routine schedule, because circulating maternal antibody can neutralise the vaccine virus, so two further doses are still required. Public health units coordinate contact tracing, and any suspected case needs urgent notification with airborne precautions on arrival at a health service.
key_points: Vaccine within seventy two hours is the preferred prophylaxis for a healthy contact aged six months or over.
Immunoglobulin covers exposures beyond seventy two hours and up to six days, and vulnerable contacts.
A dose before twelve months does not replace either scheduled dose.
Serology should not delay prophylaxis after a defined exposure.
Measles remains airborne in a room for up to two hours after the case leaves.
explanation.pearls: Vitamin A is given to children with measles admitted to hospital or with severe disease, in two daily doses with a third dose after several weeks, because deficiency worsens outcomes even in high income settings where it is easily overlooked.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG
